name: MOD
description: MOD returns the remainder after dividing a number by a divisor. The sign of the result always matches the sign of the divisor.
tldr: Returns the remainder after division, with the sign of the divisor.

parameters.name: number
parameters.description: The dividend, the number to be divided.

parameters.name: divisor
parameters.description: The number by which to divide. Cannot be 0.

advancedExamples.title: Negative dividend, positive divisor
advancedExamples.description: The result takes the divisor's (positive) sign.

advancedExamples.title: Positive dividend, negative divisor
advancedExamples.description: The result takes the divisor's (negative) sign.

howItWorks: MOD computes number - divisor × INT(number / divisor). Because it uses INT, the result always has the same sign as the divisor, unlike a simple remainder that is always non-negative.

howToSteps.name: Select the cell
howToSteps.text: Click the cell for the result.

limitations: The divisor cannot be 0; MOD(n, 0) returns #DIV/0!.
The result's sign follows the divisor, which can be counter-intuitive (MOD(-3,2)=1).
Results are floating-point; tiny rounding may appear with non-integer inputs.

commonErrors.cause: Forgetting the result follows the divisor's sign.
commonErrors.fix: Apply ABS if you need a non-negative remainder, or adjust signs intentionally.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: MOD works identically in Google Sheets, including the sign-follows-divisor rule.

faq.question: Why is MOD(-3, 2) equal to 1?
faq.answer: MOD returns a result with the same sign as the divisor. Since the divisor 2 is positive, the remainder is positive 1.

faq.question: Is MOD the same as a programming remainder?
faq.answer: Not always. In many languages '%' gives a sign matching the dividend; Excel's MOD matches the divisor.

faq.question: How do I get a non-negative remainder?
faq.answer: Wrap with ABS: =ABS(MOD(number, divisor)), or use MOD(MOD(number, d)+d, d) to keep it in [0, d).
